title: Live Answer Lab
subtitle: Demo assignment
company_note: Every question is about Pedalwise, a made-up bike-share company.

questions.title: Pick the right metric
questions.prompt: Pedalwise tests a new home screen in its bike-share app. Version B raises taps on the 'Unlock a bike' button by 8% compared with version A, but completed rides per user are the same in both versions. The product team wants to declare B the winner. Explain why tap rate may be the wrong success metric here, and say what Pedalwise should measure instead.
questions.reference_answer: Tap rate is a proxy, not the outcome Pedalwise cares about. More taps can come from a more prominent or more confusing button, accidental taps, or riders tapping again after a failed unlock, so taps can rise while nothing valuable changes. The business goal is rides and the revenue they bring, and completed rides did not move, so B has not shown any business value. Pedalwise should choose its primary metric before the test, such as completed rides or revenue per user, judge B on that metric, and use tap rate only as a secondary, diagnostic signal.

jev.instructions: Does the student's answer correctly explain (1) why tap rate is a poor success metric here, namely that it is a proxy that can rise without the real business outcome (rides or revenue) changing, and (2) what Pedalwise should measure instead, namely a business outcome such as completed rides, revenue per user, or retention, ideally chosen before the test? Any wording is fine. An answer covering only one of the two ideas is incomplete. The student may still be mid-answer; judge based on what has been written so far.

criteria.true: Explains that taps are a proxy that can rise without more rides or revenue, and names a business outcome to measure instead, or is clearly heading toward both.
criteria.false: Reasoning is wrong or backwards, covers only one of the two ideas, agrees that B should win on taps, or is just keywords with no explanation.

questions.title: Read the coefficients
questions.prompt: Pedalwise fits a logit model to customers' choices between membership plans. The coefficient on 'includes e-bikes' is 0.60, and the coefficient on monthly price is -0.03 per dollar. A manager says, 'So customers value e-bike access at 60 cents.' Explain the manager's mistake and work out what customers are actually willing to pay for e-bike access.
questions.reference_answer: Logit coefficients are in units of utility, not dollars, so 0.60 cannot be read as 60 cents. The price coefficient converts utility into dollars: each extra dollar of monthly price lowers utility by 0.03. Willingness to pay for a feature is its coefficient divided by the size of the price coefficient: 0.60 / 0.03 = $20 per month. So customers value e-bike access at about $20 a month.

jev.instructions: Does the student's answer correctly explain (1) that logit coefficients are measured in utility, not dollars, so 0.60 is not 60 cents, and (2) that willingness to pay is the feature coefficient divided by the absolute value of the price coefficient, which gives 0.60 / 0.03 = $20 per month? Any wording is fine. An answer covering only one of the two ideas is incomplete. The student may still be mid-answer; judge based on what has been written so far.

criteria.true: Identifies the utility-versus-dollars mistake and reaches about $20 per month by dividing by the price coefficient, or is clearly heading toward both.
criteria.false: Accepts 60 cents, reaches a willingness to pay other than about $20 per month, uses the wrong formula, covers only one of the two ideas, or is just keywords.

questions.title: Fix the AI's chatbot explanation
questions.prompt: Pedalwise wants to add an AI chatbot, built on a large language model, to answer riders' questions about prices and rules. Explain in plain terms how the chatbot produces its answers, and what it can and cannot be trusted to do.
questions.reference_answer: A large language model writes its answer one word at a time, predicting the text most likely to come next from patterns it learned in training. It does not look answers up in a database. It does not know Pedalwise's current prices or rules unless that information is given to it, for example in its instructions or in documents it can search. Because it predicts plausible text, it can state wrong information confidently, such as a made-up price or rule; this is called a hallucination. So Pedalwise should give it the official prices and rules, test it, and send questions it can't answer reliably to a person.
questions.seed_answer: The chatbot works by looking up the correct answer in a giant database of facts, the same way a search engine does. Because it was trained on the whole internet, it automatically knows Pedalwise's current prices and rules. Since it is a computer program, it never makes things up: if it does not know something, it always says so.

mistakes.error: The chatbot looks up answers in a database of facts, like a search engine.
mistakes.fix: It writes its answer by predicting likely next words from patterns it learned in training.

mistakes.error: The chatbot automatically knows Pedalwise's current prices and rules from its training.
mistakes.fix: It only knows Pedalwise's prices and rules if that information is given to it, for example in its instructions or in documents it can search.

mistakes.error: The chatbot never makes things up and always says when it does not know.
mistakes.fix: It can state wrong information confidently, for example a made-up price or rule (a hallucination).

jev.instructions: Is the AI's answer fully correct? It must explain that the chatbot produces answers by predicting likely text from patterns learned in training rather than looking them up, that it only knows Pedalwise's prices and rules if they are given to it, and that it can state wrong information confidently. Mark it false if any statement in the AI's answer is factually wrong, even if the rest is correct.

criteria.true: Every claim is correct and all three points are covered.
criteria.false: Contains at least one false claim, or leaves out one of the three points.

questions.title: Read the train/test gap
questions.prompt: Pedalwise trains a model to predict which docking stations will run out of bikes in the next hour. The model is 99% accurate on its training data but only 71% accurate on held-out data it never saw. Explain what this gap means and one thing the team could do about it.
questions.reference_answer: The gap means the model is overfitting: it has memorized patterns and noise that are specific to the training data instead of learning patterns that carry over to new stations and hours. The 99% training score overstates how good it is; the 71% held-out score is the honest estimate of how it will do in practice. The team could use a simpler model with fewer features or shallower trees, add regularization, collect more training data, or choose the model's complexity using a validation set or cross-validation, keeping the test set untouched until the final check.

jev.instructions: Does the student's answer correctly explain (1) that the gap means overfitting, so the model fits the training data, including its noise, too closely and does not generalize, which makes the held-out score the honest estimate, and (2) at least one valid remedy, such as a simpler model, regularization, more training data, or choosing complexity with a validation set or cross-validation? Any wording is fine. An answer covering only one of the two ideas is incomplete. The student may still be mid-answer; judge based on what has been written so far.

criteria.true: Identifies overfitting (or memorizing the training data) and gives at least one valid remedy, or is clearly heading toward both.
criteria.false: Gives a wrong diagnosis (for example underfitting, or blaming the held-out data), gives no valid remedy, suggests a remedy that makes overfitting worse such as a more complex model, or is just keywords.

questions.title: Fix the AI's smart contract
questions.prompt: Pedalwise wants to hold each rider's $50 bike deposit in a smart contract and refund it automatically when the bike is returned to a station. Explain how this would work and describe one real limitation.
questions.reference_answer: When a rental starts, the smart contract takes the $50 deposit and holds it. The contract cannot see the physical world, so it relies on an outside data source, called an oracle: here, the docking station reporting that the bike was returned. When the oracle reports a return within the rental window, the contract automatically refunds the deposit to the rider with no staff involved; if no return is reported in time, the contract keeps the deposit. The rule is enforced by code, so riders do not have to trust Pedalwise to issue refunds. A real limitation is that the contract is only as reliable as the oracle: if a dock is faulty, offline, or tampered with, the contract refunds or keeps deposits wrongly even though its own code ran correctly. Another is that deployed contract code generally cannot be edited, so changing the rules means deploying a new contract or using an upgrade mechanism planned in advance.
questions.seed_answer: When a rental starts, the smart contract takes the rider's $50 deposit and holds it. Because the contract runs on the blockchain, it can detect by itself when the bike is docked at a station, so no outside data is needed. When it sees the bike return, it refunds the deposit automatically. Since the refund rule is written in code, it can never refund the wrong rider or keep a deposit by mistake. If Pedalwise later wants to change the deposit amount or the rental window, it can simply edit the deployed contract, just like updating a normal app.

mistakes.error: The smart contract can detect the bike's return by itself, so no outside data is needed.
mistakes.fix: The contract cannot see the physical world; it relies on an outside data source (an oracle), such as the dock reporting the return.

mistakes.error: Because the rule is written in code, the contract can never refund or keep a deposit by mistake.
mistakes.fix: If the outside data is faulty or tampered with, the contract can refund or keep a deposit wrongly even though its code is correct.

mistakes.error: Pedalwise can simply edit the deployed contract, like updating a normal app.
mistakes.fix: Deployed contract code generally cannot be edited; changing the rules means deploying a new contract or using an upgrade mechanism planned in advance.

jev.instructions: Is the AI's answer fully correct? It must explain that the contract holds the deposit and refunds it automatically based on a return reported by an outside data source (an oracle), and describe a real limitation, such as dependence on that data source or deployed code being hard to change. Mark it false if any statement in the AI's answer is factually wrong, even if the rest is correct.

criteria.true: Every claim is correct, the mechanism relies on an outside data source, and a real limitation is described.
criteria.false: Contains at least one false claim, or leaves out the outside data source or the limitation.
